column2: Why does high humidity reduce evaporative cooling even though sweat is produced?
column3: Evaporation cools only if sweat reaches the skin and vapour pressure permits it; with high humidity, sweat drips unevaporated and removes little heat.

column2: Why does heart rate rise during prolonged exercise in the heat?
column3: Skin blood flow competes with active muscle and central blood volume, and sweating reduces plasma volume, so stroke volume can fall and heart rate rises.

column3: Plasma volume expands, sweating starts earlier and is more distributed, and aldosterone-mediated sodium conservation makes sweat more dilute.

column2: What feature distinguishes heat stroke from heat exhaustion, and why does continued sweating not exclude it?
column3: Heat stroke combines dangerous hyperthermia with central nervous system dysfunction; normal-looking skin or ongoing sweating does not rule it out, so rapid cooling should not wait.

column2: Why do antipyretics not correct heat stroke?
column3: Unlike fever, heat stroke does not involve an elevated hypothalamic set point, so lowering the set point does not address the heat imbalance.

column2: Why is the initial hypoxic ventilatory response at altitude restrained, and how is sustained hyperventilation permitted over days?
column3: Hyperventilation lowers carbon dioxide and causes respiratory alkalosis, which restrains further ventilation; over days the kidney excretes bicarbonate, allowing sustained hyperventilation.

column2: Why do astronauts often develop orthostatic intolerance on return to gravity?
